question_text:
A 69-year-old African American man is brought to the emergency department with sudden onset lower limb paralysis and back pain. He has had generalized bone pain for 2 months. He has no history of severe illnesses. He takes ibuprofen for pain. On examination, he is pale. The vital signs include: temperature 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse 68/min, respiratory rate 16/min, and blood pressure 155/90 mm Hg. The neurologic examination shows paraparesis. The 8th thoracic vertebra is tender to palpation. An X-ray of the thoracic vertebrae confirms a compression fracture at the same level. The laboratory studies show the following:
Laboratory test
Hemoglobin 9 g/dL
Mean corpuscular volume 95 μm3
Leukocyte count 5,000/mm3
Platelet count 240,000/mm3
ESR 85 mm/hour
Serum
Na+ 135 mEq/L
K+ 4.2 mEq/L
Cl− 113 mEq/L
HCO3− 20 mEq/L
Ca+ 11.5 mg/dL
Albumin 4 g/dL
Urea nitrogen 18 mg/dL
Creatinine 1.2 mg/dL
Serum electrophoresis shows a monoclonal protein level of 38 g/L. To reduce the likelihood of fracture recurrence, it is most appropriate to administer which of the following?

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient is a 69-year-old African American man presenting with lower limb paralysis, back pain, and a confirmed compression fracture at T8. Laboratory findings indicate anemia (hemoglobin 9 g/dL), elevated ESR (85 mm/hour), and hypercalcemia (calcium 11.5 mg/dL), alongside a monoclonal protein level of 38 g/L, suggesting a diagnosis of multiple myeloma. This condition is associated with an increased risk of fractures due to bone density loss. Pamidronate, a bisphosphonate, is indicated for reducing bone resorption and increasing bone density, thereby preventing further fractures in patients with multiple myeloma. Other options such as calcitonin, calcitriol, fluoride, and testosterone do not have the same level of evidence supporting their use for fracture prevention in this context. Therefore, the most appropriate choice for this patient is Pamidronate.
